privacyPolicy.title: Privacy Policy
privacyPolicy.description: Perintis's privacy policy, by Rhazes Labs.
privacyPolicy.intro: Perintis ("we") is developed by Rhazes Labs. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, store, and protect your personal data when you use Perintis, in line with Indonesia's Law No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection ("PDP Law"). By using Perintis, you agree to the practices described in this policy.

sections.heading: 1. Data Controller
sections.body: Rhazes Labs acts as the data controller for personal data collected through Perintis. Questions or requests regarding your personal data can be sent through the contact listed in the "Contact Us" section of this policy.

sections.heading: 2. Personal Data We Collect
sections.body: We collect data you provide directly, as well as data generated from your use of the service, including:
list: Account data: your email address and encrypted password when you register through Supabase Auth.

Career profile data: full name, phone number, location, LinkedIn/portfolio links, professional summary, work experience, education, skills, certifications, projects, and languages that you enter yourself.
Resume files and text: PDF/DOCX files you upload for the ATS Compatibility Check and CV Import features, plus the text extracted from those files.
Job posting data: job description text you optionally paste in for the keyword-match analysis feature.
Resumes you build: content created through the Resume Builder feature.
Technical data: IP address, device and browser type, and access logs collected automatically for security and service maintenance.

sections.heading: 3. How We Use Your Data
sections.body: We use your personal data to:
list: Provide and operate Perintis's core features, including Profile, Resume Builder, and ATS Compatibility Check.
Automatically analyze your resume (document structure, contact-info completeness, writing strength, and keyword match against a job posting) using artificial intelligence technology.
Authenticate your account and maintain the security of your login session.
Communicate with you about your account, service updates, or support requests.
Comply with applicable legal obligations.

sections.heading: 4. Legal Basis for Processing
sections.body: Processing of your personal data is based on: (a) your explicit consent when registering and using certain features (such as uploading a resume or job posting); (b) performance of the service contract between you and Rhazes Labs to provide the features you use; and (c) our legitimate interest in maintaining security and improving service quality.

sections.heading: 5. Third-Party Processing and Data Transfers
sections.body: To provide the service, we use the following third-party providers, which may process your data on servers located outside Indonesia:
list: Supabase, for account authentication and database storage (profile, resumes, analysis results).

Google Gemini API, for AI-powered features (resume content analysis, keyword extraction, job matching, and CV import). Relevant resume and/or job posting text is sent to Google for processing under Google AI's privacy policy and terms of service, and is not shared with any other party beyond that purpose.
We do not sell your personal data to any third party for marketing purposes.

sections.heading: 6. Data Storage and Security
sections.body: Your data is stored in a managed PostgreSQL database via Supabase, with encryption in transit (HTTPS/TLS) and authentication-based access control. We apply reasonable technical and organizational measures to protect your data from unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure, or destruction. That said, no system is completely immune to security risks.

sections.heading: 7. Data Retention
sections.body: We retain your personal data for as long as your account is active and as needed to provide the service. You may request deletion of your data or account at any time via the contact in "Contact Us". Once a deletion request is processed, your data will be removed from our production systems, except data we are legally required to retain.

sections.heading: 8. Your Rights as a Data Subject
sections.body: Under Indonesia's PDP Law, you have the right to:
list: Obtain access to and a copy of the personal data we process about you.
Complete, update, and/or correct inaccurate personal data.
Terminate processing, delete, and/or destroy your personal data.
Withdraw consent you previously gave for processing your personal data.
Object to automated decision-making, including profiling.
Request the delay or restriction of processing of your personal data, proportionally.
Claim and receive compensation for violations in the processing of your personal data, as regulated by applicable law.
Lodge a complaint with the relevant Personal Data Protection supervisory authority.

sections.heading: 9. Cookies and Similar Technologies
sections.body: We use essential session cookies to maintain your login state via Supabase Auth. We do not use third-party advertising cookies or cross-site trackers for advertising purposes.

sections.heading: 10. Children's Privacy
sections.body: Perintis is intended for users aged 18 and above, or who have entered the workforce. We do not knowingly collect personal data from children under that age. If you become aware that a child's data has been collected without valid consent, please contact us for prompt deletion.

sections.heading: 11. Changes to This Policy
sections.body: We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time to reflect changes in the service or legal requirements. Material changes will be communicated through the app or by email before taking effect. The "Last updated" date above reflects the most recent revision.

sections.heading: 12. Contact Us
sections.body: For questions, data access/deletion requests, or privacy-related complaints, please contact us at rhazesd@gmail.com.

ats-friendly-resume.title: How to Write a Resume That Actually Passes an ATS
ats-friendly-resume.excerpt: Most resumes never reach a human. Here's how to make sure yours does.

sections.heading: Why formatting matters more than you think
sections.body: An Applicant Tracking System (ATS) reads your resume before any recruiter does. It's parsing software, not a person, and it can only read what it's built to read. A resume that looks perfectly clean on your screen can come out as a jumbled mess once an ATS tries to extract your work history from it.

sections.heading: Stick to a single column
sections.body: Multi-column layouts and text boxes are the most common cause of ATS parsing failures. Most parsers read left to right, top to bottom, in a single stream, so a two-column layout can scramble your work experience and education into the wrong order, or drop sections entirely. A single-column layout is the safest choice.

sections.heading: Avoid tables, images, and headers/footers for key info
sections.body: Tables are structured for visual layout, not for a parser trying to extract plain text. The same goes for your contact information: if it's placed inside a header or footer, some ATS parsers skip it entirely, meaning a recruiter's system might not even register that you have a phone number or email.

sections.heading: Use standard section headings
sections.body: "Work Experience", "Education", "Skills": these are the headings ATS parsers are trained to recognize. Creative alternatives like "Where I've Been" or "My Journey" might read fine to a human, but risk confusing the parser about what section it's looking at.

sections.heading: Test it before you send it
sections.body: The only way to know for sure how your resume parses is to run it through an actual ATS-style check. Perintis' ATS Compatibility Check scans your resume for exactly these issues, tables, columns, non-standard fonts, missing contact info, and gives you a clear score with what to fix.

cover-letter-mistakes.title: 5 Cover Letter Mistakes That Get Applications Ignored
cover-letter-mistakes.excerpt: A generic cover letter is often worse than no cover letter at all. Here's what to avoid.

sections.heading: 1. Starting with "To Whom It May Concern"
sections.body: A generic salutation signals a generic letter. If the job posting or company website lists a hiring manager or team name, use it. If not, "Dear [Company] Hiring Team" already reads as more specific and more effort than a placeholder greeting.

sections.heading: 2. Repeating your resume instead of adding to it
sections.body: A cover letter that just restates your job titles and dates wastes the reader's time, they already have your resume. Use the space to explain why this specific role and company matter to you, and connect one or two of your strongest achievements directly to what the posting is asking for.

sections.heading: 3. Writing more than one page
sections.body: Recruiters skim. A cover letter longer than 3-4 short paragraphs is more likely to be skipped than read in full. Say what matters, then stop.

sections.heading: 4. Never mentioning the company or role by name
sections.body: A letter that could be sent to any company for any job reads exactly like what it is: a template. Reference something specific, the role's responsibilities, the company's product, a detail from the job posting, to show the letter was actually written for this application.

sections.heading: 5. Ending without a clear close
sections.body: "I look forward to hearing from you" is a fine closing line, but pair it with confidence, not just politeness. State plainly that you're excited about the opportunity and available to discuss it further.

resume-scan-time.title: The Truth About How Long Recruiters Actually Look at Your Resume
resume-scan-time.excerpt: The "6-second resume" myth isn't quite right, but the real number should still change how you write.

sections.heading: Where the "6-second" number actually comes from
sections.body: You've probably heard some version of "recruiters only look at your resume for 6 seconds." The number traces back to a 2018 eye-tracking study by TheLadders, which found an average of 7.4 seconds for a recruiter's first pass through a resume. That's a real, widely cited figure, not internet folklore, but it describes one specific moment: the initial screening glance, not the total time a resume that clears that first cut gets reviewed.

sections.heading: What that first glance is actually judging
sections.body: In those first seconds, a recruiter isn't reading your resume the way you'd read an article. Eye-tracking data shows they scan for a handful of anchor points: your most recent job title and company, your current or most recent role's dates, and whether the layout looks organized enough to trust. If nothing in that scan earns a second look, the rest of the resume, however strong, may never get read.

sections.heading: Design for the scan, not just the read
sections.body: This is why layout choices matter as much as content. Your most recent, most relevant role should be immediately visible without scrolling or hunting. Job titles and company names should stand out visually from dates and descriptions. Dense paragraphs are easy to skip; short, specific bullet points are easier to scan and land.

sections.heading: The good news: a strong resume earns more time
sections.body: The 7-second figure isn't a hard ceiling, it's a filter. A resume that passes that first scan gets a real, longer read afterward. The goal isn't to cram your entire story into 7 seconds; it's to make sure the most convincing, relevant information is what a recruiter's eyes land on first.

quantify-achievements.title: How to Quantify Your Achievements When You Don't Have Exact Numbers
quantify-achievements.excerpt: "Increased revenue" says nothing. Here's how to add real numbers, even in roles that don't naturally produce them.

sections.heading: Why recruiters trust numbers over adjectives
sections.body: "Improved team efficiency" could mean almost anything. "Cut onboarding time from 3 weeks to 9 days" tells a specific, verifiable story. Numbers give a recruiter something concrete to evaluate instead of asking them to take your word for it.

sections.heading: Start with what you can count, not what you measured
sections.body: You don't need a formal KPI dashboard to quantify a bullet. Team size you managed, number of projects delivered, frequency of a task, size of a budget you were responsible for, all of these are countable even if you never tracked a formal metric at the time.

sections.heading: Estimate honestly when exact figures aren't available
sections.body: If you genuinely don't have the exact number, a reasonable, honest estimate is still more useful than none. "Supported a team of roughly 15 people" or "handled an estimated 30-40 support tickets weekly" is defensible and specific. What matters is that the estimate is genuine, not a number invented to sound impressive.

sections.heading: Numbers alone aren't the whole story
sections.body: A number without context can undersell you. "Increased signups by 12%" is stronger when it's clear that's against a flat baseline, or came during a period with a shrinking marketing budget. Where it's relevant, briefly note the context that makes the number meaningful.

hard-skills-vs-soft-skills.title: Hard Skills vs. Soft Skills: What Actually Belongs on Your Resume
hard-skills-vs-soft-skills.excerpt: Both matter, but they don't belong in the same place, or written the same way.

sections.heading: The difference, quickly
sections.body: Hard skills are specific, teachable, and usually verifiable: a programming language, a certification, fluency in a tool like Excel or Figma. Soft skills are behavioral: communication, leadership, adaptability. Both matter to employers, but they need very different treatment on a resume.

sections.heading: Hard skills: be specific and list them plainly
sections.body: A dedicated Skills section works well for hard skills because they're exactly what an ATS keyword search and a recruiter's skim are both looking for. List them plainly: "SQL", "Adobe Premiere Pro", "Google Analytics", rather than folding them into a sentence where a keyword scan might miss them.

sections.heading: Soft skills: show them, don't just claim them
sections.body: Writing "strong communicator" as a bullet point is easy to write and easy to ignore, everyone claims it. Soft skills land better when they're demonstrated through an achievement: "Led weekly cross-team syncs between design and engineering to resolve scope conflicts" shows communication and leadership without naming either word.

sections.heading: Match the mix to the role
sections.body: A technical role weighted toward hard skills still needs a couple of demonstrated soft skills, most jobs involve working with other people. A people-facing role heavy on soft skills still benefits from listing the specific tools and platforms you're fluent in. Neither category should be entirely absent.

resume-length.title: One Page or Two? How Long Your Resume Should Actually Be
resume-length.excerpt: The one-page rule isn't dead, but it's not universal either. Here's what actually determines the right length.

sections.heading: The old rule, and why it's changing
sections.body: "Keep it to one page" made sense when resumes were printed and physically handed across a desk. Today, most resumes are read on a screen or parsed by software, and a well-organized second page costs a reader nothing extra. A 2025 survey of over 1,000 HR professionals found the majority now consider one to two pages acceptable, a real shift from the old single-page-only expectation.

sections.heading: Length should follow experience, not a fixed rule
sections.body: The most useful guideline ties length to career stage: candidates with under five years of experience generally fit comfortably on one page, and forcing more onto it usually means padding. Candidates with five or more years of relevant experience, especially with multiple roles worth describing in detail, often need two pages to do that experience justice without cutting real substance.

sections.heading: A second page only helps if every line earns its place
sections.body: Two pages is not permission to include everything. Every bullet still has to compete for a recruiter's limited attention. If a line doesn't support your case for this specific role, it doesn't belong, whether it's page one or page two.

sections.heading: When in doubt, cut before you extend
sections.body: If you're unsure whether an entry justifies a second page, try cutting it first. A tight one-page resume beats a two-page resume padded with filler nearly every time.

career-gap.title: How to Explain a Career Gap Without Apologizing for It
career-gap.excerpt: A gap in your resume isn't automatically a red flag, how you frame it is what matters.

sections.heading: Recruiters see gaps more often than you think
sections.body: Career breaks for caregiving, health, layoffs, further study, or a difficult job market are common, not rare exceptions. Most recruiters have seen far more gaps than perfectly continuous timelines. The problem isn't usually the gap itself, it's an unexplained gap that reads as something being hidden.

sections.heading: Address it briefly, don't over-explain
sections.body: A short, factual line is enough: "Took a 10-month career break for family caregiving" or "Focused on an intensive certification program from March to November." You don't owe a lengthy justification. Over-explaining can accidentally signal more insecurity about the gap than the gap itself does.

sections.heading: If you used the time productively, say so, briefly
sections.body: If the gap included freelance work, volunteering, coursework, or a personal project, a one-line mention adds useful context without turning it into the centerpiece of your resume. If it didn't, that's fine too, honesty reads better than a stretched explanation.

sections.heading: Let your interview do the rest of the talking
sections.body: The resume doesn't need to resolve every question about a gap, it just needs to not raise unnecessary alarm. Save the fuller story, and your confidence in telling it, for the interview itself.

linkedin-vs-resume.title: LinkedIn Profile vs. Resume: What's Different, and Why It Matters
linkedin-vs-resume.excerpt: They tell the same career story, but for different readers, at different moments.

sections.heading: Different readers, different intent
sections.body: A resume is read by someone who already has a specific role in mind and is deciding whether you fit it. A LinkedIn profile is often the first thing a recruiter finds before any role is on the table, or the thing a hiring manager checks after your resume already made an impression. Same person, different job.

sections.heading: Your resume should be sharp; your LinkedIn can be broader
sections.body: A resume works best tailored tightly to one role, trimmed to what's relevant. LinkedIn has room to be more complete: past roles you're not actively pitching for a current application, projects and interests that show range, recommendations from former colleagues that a resume can't carry.

sections.heading: Keep the facts consistent, even if the framing differs
sections.body: Job titles, company names, and dates should match between the two. A mismatch, even an innocent one from an old update, is one of the fastest ways to make a recruiter double back and scrutinize everything else more closely.

sections.heading: Use LinkedIn to do what a resume can't
sections.body: A resume can't show ongoing activity, but a LinkedIn profile can: posts, comments, and engagement in your field signal that you're active and current, not just a static document. It's also the place recommendations and endorsements actually add credibility a resume alone can't provide.

cover-letter-tone.title: Formal or Casual? How to Match Your Cover Letter's Tone to the Company
cover-letter-tone.excerpt: The same achievements, written the wrong way, can make you look like the wrong fit.

sections.heading: Tone signals fit before content does
sections.body: A recruiter reading your cover letter is unconsciously asking a second question alongside "can they do the job": "would they fit here?" A stiff, overly formal letter to a scrappy startup can read as out of step with the culture, just as an overly casual letter to a conservative corporate or state-owned enterprise can read as underprepared.

sections.heading: Read the job posting for tone cues, not just requirements
sections.body: A job posting itself is a tone sample. Formal, structured language with a lot of qualification requirements usually signals a formal reading is safer. Casual, personality-driven copy, especially at startups, is often an invitation to write with some of that same energy back.

sections.heading: Formal doesn't mean stiff, and casual doesn't mean unprofessional
sections.body: A formal cover letter can still be warm and specific, it just avoids slang and keeps sentence structure more traditional. A casual cover letter still needs to be well-written and typo-free, casual is a register, not a license to be careless.

sections.heading: When you're not sure, default slightly more formal
sections.body: It's easier to recover from a cover letter that reads as a little more polished than the company culture than one that reads as underdressed for it. If the signals are mixed, leaning formal is the safer default.

tailor-resume-per-job.title: How to Tailor One Resume for Different Jobs Without Starting From Scratch
tailor-resume-per-job.excerpt: You don't need a brand new resume for every application, you need one that adapts fast.

sections.heading: Why a single generic resume underperforms
sections.body: A resume written to apply broadly, to nothing in particular, ends up speaking clearly to no one. Recruiters and ATS keyword matches both respond to specificity: language that mirrors the actual posting, achievements framed around what this particular role cares about.

sections.heading: Build a master version first
sections.body: Keep one comprehensive version of your resume, with every role, bullet, and achievement you might ever want to use. This isn't the version you send anywhere, it's your source material. Tailoring becomes a matter of selecting and reordering from this master, not writing from a blank page each time.

sections.heading: Match language to the job posting, not just responsibilities
sections.body: If a posting says "stakeholder management" and your master resume says "worked with clients", align the wording. This isn't dishonest, it's translating your real experience into the vocabulary the reader, and the ATS scanning for it, is actually looking for.

sections.heading: Reorder before you rewrite
sections.body: The fastest tailoring often isn't new writing, it's reordering. Move your most relevant bullets and roles higher, push less relevant ones lower or cut them for this specific application. A recruiter's first scan matters most, put your best match for this job where that scan will land.
